solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Band wanting sex and drug experience

blocks.note: the opening letter of 'sex', the usual single-letter abbreviation
a trip is a hallucinogenic drug experience

explanation.surface: A rock group on tour doing without sex but not without drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like a pop group but is the definition in its other sense, a long narrow piece; 'wanting' only joins it to the wordplay, and the answer also teases the sex theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip and a band are both long narrow pieces of material, such as a strip of cloth or tape.

clue.text: A peer makes one phone call

blocks.note: read 'peer' as one who pees; the childish word for a wee is wanted
British informal for a ring on the telephone

explanation.surface: A member of the House of Lords picking up the telephone to ring someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a lord, but split it as pee-er, somebody urinating; a tinkle is childish slang for a wee. In Britain 'give me a tinkle' also means give me a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are informal British slang: a childish word for urinating and a colloquial term for a telephone ring.

clue.text: One beer ain't affecting a piss-artist

indicators.note: the letters are acted upon and altered, so the drink words get rearranged

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker insisting one pint has no effect on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' must become the numeral I before the letters are mixed; 'ain't' contributes its four letters without the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Piss-artist is crude British slang for a habitual drunk, and an inebriate is a formal noun for such a person.

clue.text: Like drugs? Dicky did when on the go outside

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the next word is in a broken order
the phrase 'on the go' is placed around the jumbled word

explanation.surface: Someone named Dicky dabbling in drugs while always busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a man's name but is British slang for shaky or faulty, so it tells you to scramble 'did'; 'when' is only a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Drugs are habit-forming, so something addictive is like drugs; the question mark admits the definition is by example.

clue.text: Shit! Long time lockdown sufferer's dark place

explanation.surface: Someone cursing the endless pandemic lockdown and their gloomy mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shit!' reads as an exclamation but is a noun; the definition treats a prisoner locked in as a 'lockdown sufferer'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground prison cell, a gloomy place where captives are shut away.

clue.text: Boris's description of a certain special relationship: "upset bride with insult, etc"

definitions.text: Boris's description of a certain special relationship
definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adjective: the word Boris used

indicators.note: things knocked over end up out of order, so the words that follow are scrambled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters; 'with' joins the pieces

explanation.surface: A satirical quote about Boris Johnson and a troubled marriage full of insults.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris Johnson, then UK Prime Minister, called the US–UK special relationship indestructible in 2021; the surface slyly hints at his own marriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson publicly used this adjective for the transatlantic alliance, calling it incapable of being broken.

clue.text: Golfer makes great start getting into row

indicators.note: a word's start is its opening letter, here of 'great'
the selected letter goes inside the word for a row

blocks.note: a row of seats, as in a stadium

explanation.surface: A golfer opening strongly and getting into a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' tempts as an argument, but it is a line of seats; Tiger Woods is the golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiger Woods is among the most famous professional players of the sport, so the name stands for a golfer by example.

clue.text: Pathetic suitor crushed by very round master

indicators.note: a pathetic effort is a poor one, so the word after it is badly arranged
squeezed between the letters for 'very' and 'round'

explanation.surface: A feeble would-be lover utterly flattened by a large, rotund boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' looks like the crusher, but it is the definition; V and O sit either side of the mixed suitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A virtuoso is a performer of outstanding skill, one who has mastered an art such as music.

clue.text: Broken, once in office? Choice president's first step

definitions.note: describes the answer rather than naming it

indicators.note: the president's first is the opening letter of that word

blocks.note: a vote is a choice between candidates
a shelf or step of rock

explanation.surface: A satirical view of a president taking office and at once going back on promises.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cynical joke: a campaign promise is typically broken once the winner takes power.
explanation.definitionFit: Campaign promises are notoriously abandoned after victory, so the cynical description identifies such a promise.

clue.text: Stressed – but showing less than your fair share of wrinkles?

definitions.text: showing less than your fair share of wrinkles?

blocks.note: emphasised, as a word with a line drawn beneath it

blocks.clueFragment: showing less than your fair share of wrinkles?
blocks.note: split the answer in two: too few lines on the face

explanation.surface: An anxious person oddly free of the wrinkles worry should bring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stressed' looks like anxiety but means emphasised; the second half splits the answer into UNDER and LINED.
explanation.definitionFit: Text given emphasis has a line ruled beneath it, while a face with few creases is humorously short of lines.

clue.text: Bloody work – royalty disheartened

indicators.note: losing the heart takes away everything between the ends, keeping only the outside of 'royalty'

blocks.note: to function, as a machine does

explanation.surface: A grim job that has left the royal family dispirited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' reads as a noun, but as a verb it means operate, which 'go' also means.
explanation.definitionFit: Gory and bloody both describe scenes full of violence and spilled blood.

clue.text: Minister's corrupt circle

indicators.note: corrupted things are spoiled from their proper form, so the word that follows is mixed up

explanation.surface: A government minister's crooked inner clique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests a politician, but here it is a church minister; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is a member of the clergy, which is exactly what a cleric is.

clue.text: Hours wasted in final cover up

indicators.note: wasted means drunk and out of shape, so the letters of 'hours' stagger
the jumbled letters go inside the word for 'final'

explanation.surface: Time frittered away during the last stage of a scandal's concealment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover up' suggests a scandal, but here it is the plain verb for wrapping something entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshroud is to wrap in a shroud, hiding something completely from view.

clue.text: Put in line following Macron's lead – which is rubbish

indicators.note: the lead of a word is the letter at its front, here of 'Macron's'

blocks.note: positional word: what comes next goes after the M

explanation.surface: Falling into line behind President Macron, which the writer thinks is nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish' reads as a noun but is the verb, meaning to criticise; the definition is at the end, after 'which is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish someone is British informal for disparaging them, and to malign is to speak ill of them unfairly.

clue.text: Have a lie-down ... er, to get round model

indicators.note: turning something round points it the other way, so 'er' is read backwards

blocks.note: a model poses for an artist

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly saying they'll rest before getting to a model.
explanation.walkthrough: The hesitant 'er' looks like filler but supplies two letters; 'model' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To repose is to lie at rest, a formal way of saying to recline and relax.

clue.text: Note: it somehow enters China as a possibility

indicators.note: arranged in some unstated way, so 'note' and 'it' are mixed
the mixed letters go inside the word that 'China' gives

blocks.note: cockney rhyming slang: china plate means mate

explanation.surface: A memo about something getting into China, raised as a possible scenario.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but in cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, so china is a pal.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential and possibility both mean a capacity that may develop in the future.

clue.text: Prince on vacation in West Country resort – a means of evasion

indicators.note: the prince and his holiday are placed inside the resort's name

blocks.note: British short form of holiday; 'on' puts it after the prince
Looe is a seaside town in Cornwall

explanation.surface: A royal on holiday in the south-west of England, dodging something.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is south-west England; Looe is a Cornish fishing town. 'On vacation' feels like one phrase but splits into 'on' and HOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A loophole is a gap in a rule that lets someone escape an obligation, so it is a way of evading.

clue.text: What Boris is supposed to do with one of his ministers – rotten, gutless

definitions.text: What Boris is supposed to do

indicators.note: without guts means the insides are gone, keeping only the ends of 'rotten'

blocks.note: Michael Gove, a minister in Boris Johnson's cabinet

explanation.surface: A jibe that Boris Johnson's cabinet is rotten and spineless.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Gove was a senior minister under Prime Minister Boris Johnson; the definition mocks Johnson for not doing his job.
explanation.definitionFit: A prime minister is meant to run the country, and to govern is to rule a state.

clue.text: Hoover put away – clear off

blocks.note: a Hoover is a vacuum cleaner, a vac for short
put away as in eat up food

explanation.surface: Put the vacuum cleaner away and get out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'Hoover' is used generically for a vacuum cleaner; 'put away' means stored but here means consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: To vacate a place is to leave it empty, the same as to depart from it.

clue.text: Steven is on-screen – in possession of a joint?

indicators.note: the words hold the answer within them, as one possesses it

explanation.surface: Someone called Steven appearing on television while holding a cannabis joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' tempts as cannabis, but it is a cut of meat; the question mark marks venison as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Venison is deer meat, and a haunch of it roasted is a joint in the butcher's sense.

clue.text: Underwear items – they don't make a big statement

definitions.text: they don't make a big statement

blocks.clueFragment: they don't make a big statement
blocks.note: short summaries or instructions, kept concise

explanation.surface: Pants that are modest and discreet rather than showy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads as fashion, but it is the plural of the noun for a short summary.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefs are close-fitting underpants, and a brief is also a short written statement of instructions or facts.

clue.text: 'Love cage' project for a possible house layout

explanation.surface: A 'love cage' scheme as a proposal for designing a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love cage' looks like a single odd phrase but divides into two pieces; 'project' is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-plan describes interiors with few internal walls, a common arrangement of rooms in a home.

clue.text: Writer standing up against a large kingdom

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up turns the word bottom to top

blocks.note: positional word: next to, so the pieces sit side by side

explanation.surface: An author taking a stand against a big monarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' is not an author but an instrument; Nepal was a kingdom until 2008, which is why the clue calls it one.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepal, the Himalayan country, was ruled by a monarchy until becoming a republic in 2008.

clue.text: Disregard Italian bloke, going topless

indicators.note: losing the top means the first letter of the Italian word goes

blocks.note: Italian for a man or gentleman

explanation.surface: Pay no attention to an Italian man who has taken his shirt off.
explanation.walkthrough: Signore is the Italian form of address for a gentleman; dropping its S leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Disregard and ignore are straightforward synonymous verbs for paying no attention.

clue.text: Get into a lather when a fool grabs Obama's top

indicators.note: the top of a word is its opening letter, here of 'Obama's'
the fool's word seizes and holds the letter inside it

blocks.note: a sap is a gullible person

explanation.surface: Getting worked up when some idiot snatches Barack Obama's shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get into a lather' reads as getting agitated, but taken literally it means to cover with suds.
explanation.definitionFit: To soap something is to rub it with cleanser so that it foams, covering it in suds.

clue.text: Hell! Declaration by Brenda amounts to refusal to accept responsibility

blocks.note: Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth, whose royal cipher is ER; 'by' sets it beside the claim

explanation.surface: An exasperated reaction to the Queen issuing a statement dodging blame.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the late Queen 'Brenda', so she gives ER (Elizabeth Regina); 'Hell!' is an exclamation but gives the underworld's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A disclaimer is a formal statement denying liability, so it amounts to refusing to take responsibility.

clue.text: Weak politician welcomes all men, perhaps, with the best of intentions

indicators.note: perhaps signals the words are one possible arrangement, so 'all men' is to be rearranged
the politician's word takes the others inside itself as a host takes guests

blocks.note: a wet is a moderate, soft Conservative, a Thatcher-era term

explanation.surface: A feeble MP inviting in every man, meaning well.
explanation.walkthrough: In British politics a 'wet' is a moderate Tory seen as weak, a word from Margaret Thatcher's era.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done with kindly intent, even if it misfires, is described as well-meant.

clue.text: Expose member, 'Gordon'?

blocks.note: to reveal one's private parts briefly in public
the first name of the comic-strip space hero Gordon

explanation.surface: Revealing a member of a group, perhaps named Gordon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' reads as a club member but is the anatomical sense; the question mark says Gordon wants his first name, as in Flash Gordon.
explanation.definitionFit: Flashing is indecent exposure, and the science-fiction hero's first name completes Flash Gordon.
